newsitem.title: CHINA: China planner says market needs state's helping hand.
newsitem.headline: China planner says market needs state's helping hand.

text.p: China's economic planning chief said on Thursday that despite nearly two decades of reforms, the "invisible hand" of the market still needed the helping touch of the state.
"We want to make up for the defects of the market," Chen Jinhua, head of the State Planning Commission, told reporters.

"The invisible hand of the market should be supported by the visible hand of the state," he said, in a reference to the description by 18th century economist Adam Smith of how the market's "invisible hand" matched supply and demand.
The State Planning Commission, an influential decision-making body under China's old central planning regime, has seen some of its powers trimmed with the shift to more market-oriented policies.

But it still plays a major role in setting economic policy, particularly for key industries -- such as electric power and basic infrastructure. It also has direct control over import quotas in strategic areas.
Beijing this year "would try to strike a balance between government regulation and enterprise initiatives", he said.
China's communist leaders have called for reform of the nation's struggling state enterprises to make them better able to compete in what is rapidly becoming a sink-or-swim marketplace.
Beijing has been reluctant to turn them loose entirely, fearing that failures of large state firms would put workers out on the street and lead to social unrest.
"Many state enterprises are losing money and owe banks lots of money to the banks," Chen said. "We are concerned about the bad debts of many state enterprises."
But many large state companies were operating efficiently and the worst problems stemmed from smaller firms, Chen said.
He said two interest rate cuts last year had eased the debt burden of many of these companies.

China has said 75 percent of its more than 100,000 state companies lost money last year and total losses in the government sector soared to 69 billion yuan ($8.3 billion) between January and October, a rise of 45 percent over the year-earlier period.
Chen said state guidance was necessary for the oil refining business -- one of China's pillar industries.
Too many companies were duplicating capacity and wasting the nation's resources, he said, adding that new project plans would be reviewed carefully.
"New refineries must avoid duplication," he said.
The official also said there were too many textile manufacturers in China and that the state would not encourage the setting up of new textile plants.
